_about: Correctness thresholds. These gate; timings do not.
Two kinds of number get confused in benchmark suites. A quality
difference between two engines fitting the same objective on the same
bins is small, stable, and reproducible, so a threshold on it is a real
test: cross it and something is wrong. A timing is none of those things
on a laptop with a thermal budget, so a threshold on it is a coin toss
wearing a lab coat. verify.py reads this file and decides pass or fail.
report.py prints the timings and decides nothing.
Every value here was chosen before any run, from what the two
implementations are known to differ by, and each carries its reasoning.
Loosening one after seeing a result is allowed and has to be done in a
commit that says so; editing one to make today's run green is how a
suite stops meaning anything.
Directions. `max_worse` is how much worse mojotrees may be than
LightGBM on the primary metric. Being better is not capped, but being
much better is checked too: `implausible_better` catches the case where
the two engines were not actually given the same problem, which looks
like a win and is a bug.
An absolute limit is only meaningful next to the size of the metric it
bounds. A limit larger than the metric cannot fail, and a gate that
cannot fail is worse than no gate because a green suite is read as
evidence. `_audit` below is the sweep that checks that, and it is worth
re-running whenever a scenario gains a variant: the failure it found was
not a wrong number, it was one number covering two variants whose metric
values differ by fifty times.

_audit.question: For every absolute limit in this file, how large is it against the metric's typical value on every variant of its scenario?
_audit.method: Metric values taken from the two stored runs (results/20260815T014842Z, results/20260815T023123Z, which carry the real variant of every scenario except ranking) and, for the synthetic variants those runs do not carry, from the generator's construction in generators.py. Ratio is limit divided by LightGBM's metric value, so a ratio near or above 1 is a gate that cannot fail.
findings: imbalanced_binary / average_precision / primary: 0.02 absolute against 0.6814 real (2.9%) and against ~0.0136 synthetic (147%). BROKEN on the synthetic variant, and the implausible_better of 0.05 was worse (368%). FIXED in this commit by changing the kind to relative; see the scenario's changed/why_these_numbers/known_risk fields.

imbalanced_binary / auc / secondary: 0.005 absolute against 0.9510 real (0.5%). AUC is bounded near 1 on both variants and cannot collapse the way average precision does at a 0.5 percent positive rate, so an absolute band is the right kind here. Unchanged.
multiclass / accuracy / secondary: 0.01 absolute against 0.8572 real (1.2%). The synthetic variant is a softmax over seven skewed classes, so accuracy stays well above the 0.01 band. Unchanged.

ranking / ndcg@10 / primary: 0.02 absolute against 0.9914 (2.0%), and ndcg@5 0.025 against 0.9824 (2.5%). NDCG is bounded in [0, 1] and this scenario runs synthetic only, where every query is graded 0 to 4 so the metric cannot sit near zero. implausible_better of 0.05 is 5.0% and is if anything conservative for a bounded metric. Unchanged.
categorical_missing / auc / adult override: 0.01 absolute against 0.9274 (1.1%). Unchanged.

sparse_highdim / auc / primary: 0.01 absolute against 0.9938 (1.0%), and average_precision secondary 0.03 against 0.9937 (3.0%). Checked specifically because a sparse high-dimensional problem is where a rare positive class would be expected: it is not one. generators.sparse_highdim draws labels from logistic(1.5 * standardized latent), which is a balanced problem, so average precision sits near AUC on both variants. Unchanged.

defaults / device_agreement / max_abs_prediction_diff: 1e-3 absolute, but it bounds a per-ROW prediction difference rather than a metric, and verify.py already refuses to fail on it alone. Its companion primary_metric_relative of 0.005 is relative and is the gate that actually holds. Not a metric limit and not in scope. Worth recording that this is the gate that caught the Float32 average-precision regression the imbalanced_binary entry above describes, because its band was relative: it is doing its job and is deliberately untouched.

Baselines were checked separately and are a different shape: absolute_floor (0.65 auc, 0.85 auc, 0.70 auc) and absolute_improvement (0.05 ndcg) bound the metric itself rather than a difference between two metrics, so 'larger than the quantity it bounds' does not apply. None was changed.
_audit.conclusion: One broken gate, in two fields of one entry, both fixed by changing the kind to relative. Nothing else in the file has an absolute limit within an order of magnitude of its metric's value on any variant. Nothing was loosened.

accuracy_anchor.rationale: Registered 2026-08-17, replacing the peer-anchored accuracy budget as the accuracy gate. This bounds how much of OUR OWN accuracy one adopted change may silently cost, measured against a value recorded in accuracy_anchors.json for the same arm, scenario, tree count and device. It is a DIFFERENT QUANTITY from the 1 percent we quote against CatBoost and LightGBM, which was a standing distance to a competitor rather than a per-change allowance, so the number is not reused. Measured basis: our arms are bit-identical across repeats (check_determinism gates it) and the generators are pure and seeded, so this comparison has no noise floor for a subject arm and any tolerance above zero is a deliberate allowance rather than headroom. Nearest recorded evidence for the size is this file's dense_regression differential rationale, which records that tie breaking and floating-point summation order move RMSE in the third decimal place; that observation is about two different engines, so it is an upper bound on the movement being allowed for and not a measurement of it. INFERRED and not measured by anyone here: a change that only reassociates a reduction should move the metric less than 0.25 percent, which on an rmse of 0.31 is the fourth decimal place. If a legitimate reassociation trips this, the finding is that this number is wrong; move it here with the measurement that justified moving it. Tripping the gate is not a refusal to make the change, it is a refusal to make it silently: the remedy is a deliberate anchor refresh, which puts the old and the new number in one diff. implausible_better_relative exists for the reason the differential's does, in that check's words, 'Better than this is not a win, it is a sign the two engines were not actually given the same problem'; set tighter than the differential's 10 percent because this compares an arm against itself. Also inferred.

accuracy_peer.rationale: The scoreboard, and it GATES NOTHING. Andrew's standing directive of within 1 percent relative of the better of CatBoost-as-shipped and LightGBM stock+det at a matched tree count, kept unchanged in arithmetic and demoted from a gate on 2026-08-17. His words: the adoption rule 'should be about trading OUR accuracy for speed. not tied to whatever lightgbm or catboost is fucking doing'. Three reasons it could not stay a gate: it blocked changes that cost no accuracy at all, since the leaf-wise GPU arm's 1.043 to 0.839 second improvement was bit-identical work and the frontier would not rank it; it PERMITTED real accuracy loss whenever we were ahead, since the symmetric arm beating CatBoost at 799k could give away about 1.07 percent of its own accuracy and still pass; and the bar moved when somebody else shipped. Every line it writes is a note. There is deliberately no gating key here: after that ruling there is no run for which turning it back into a gate is the right thing to do.

mojotrees.scope: same scenario, device, and thread count
mojotrees.rationale: Repeat training is bit-identical by design, including on the accelerator, where the histogram reduction stays in fixed point precisely so that it is. A digest that moves is a regression in that property and is worth failing over even when the metrics are unchanged.

lightgbm.rationale: LightGBM is run with deterministic=true and a fixed seed, so repeats should match. It is reported rather than gated because it is not this project's invariant to hold.

data_agreement.rationale: Both engines rebuild the data independently in their own processes. Equal digests are what makes the comparison a comparison; unequal digests make every other number in the row meaningless, so this fails before anything else is checked.

device_agreement.rationale: The row bound is the tolerance the repository's own CPU-and-accelerator equivalence tests use for predictions, and it holds when both devices grow the same trees (the host split search guarantees that). The workload-aware AUTO strategy sends large shapes to the device split search, which trades exactly that guarantee: Float32 gain comparisons flip near-tie splits, so equally good trees can disagree on individual rows. verify.py therefore fails a row-bound breach only when the primary metric also leaves its band, and records it as a warning otherwise; the metric band is the gate that must hold in every configuration.

backend_proof.rationale: A record that says it ran on an accelerator has to carry something the trainer emitted that only a device run can produce, because every other check in this file passes on a CPU fit wearing a GPU label. One did: trainset.train_dataset_multiclass resolved the device, discarded the answer, and trained on the CPU, and the covertype rows of 20260815T023123Z were quoted in three reviews as the project's worst GPU result while being CPU timings. The refusal is deliberately the conjunction of three conditions rather than any one of them. A missing proof alone is a run nobody instrumented, not a lie. A prediction digest matching the CPU arm's alone is not a lie either: the device histogram reduction is fixed point precisely so that bit-exact agreement between backends is reachable, and gating on the digest would forbid the property the trainer is built to have. Together they are the signature. Turning this off means accepting device timings on the strength of a label.

pinning.rationale: A real-data result from unverified bytes is a result about an unknown dataset. Synthetic runs are exempt because their recipe is the pin.

differential.rationale: Same objective, same bin count, same leaf count. What is left is tie breaking in the split search and the order of floating-point summation, which moves RMSE in the third decimal place. Three percent is far above that and far below a broken model.

baseline.rationale: A model that cannot beat the training mean did not fit; two engines agreeing on a non-model would otherwise pass the differential check. Loosened from 0.20 after the first executed run (20260815T014842Z): YearPredictionMSD at the aligned budget yields 16.2% from LightGBM and 16.1% from mojotrees, so the pre-run fifth measured the dataset's difficulty, not the fit. Fifteen percent still fails a non-model while passing the fit both engines agree on.

differential.rationale: Average precision on a rare class is dominated by the ordering of a few hundred rows at the top of the ranking, so it is noisier than AUC on the same model. The band is relative because this metric's VALUE differs by fifty times between this scenario's two variants: bank_marketing sits near 0.68 and the synthetic variant, at a 0.5 percent positive rate, sits near 0.013. A relative band means the same thing on both.
differential.changed: 2026-08-16, tightened. This gate could not fail on the synthetic variant and had to be replaced rather than adjusted. Previous value: {kind: absolute, max_worse: 0.02, implausible_better: 0.05}, with the rationale 'Two percentage points absolute is the noise band; more than that is a difference in the trees.' Two points absolute is 154 percent of a metric whose value is 0.013, so the limit was larger than the quantity it bounded and no result could cross it: a 9.4 percent relative regression on the CPU arm (average precision 0.0136 to 0.0123, when per-row derivatives went to Float32) sat comfortably inside it and was caught only because device_agreement's relative band happened to be watching. The old value was written for a metric near 1 and was never wrong there, which is why the fix is a change of KIND and not a smaller number.
differential.why_these_numbers: 0.025 relative is TIGHTER than the value it replaces at every average precision below 0.8, and therefore on both variants: at bank_marketing's LightGBM value of 0.6814 it is 0.0170 absolute against the old 0.0200, and on the synthetic variant it is 0.00034 absolute against the old 0.0200, which is 59 times tighter. It fails the 9.4 percent regression above by a factor of 3.8 and leaves 7.9 times headroom over the only mojotrees-versus-LightGBM differential ever recorded on this metric (0.318 percent relative, 20260815T014842Z and 20260815T023123Z). implausible_better moves the same way for the same reason: 0.07 relative is 0.0477 absolute at bank_marketing against the old 0.05. Both are tightenings, which is the direction this file's preamble permits without a re-argument.
differential.known_risk: No mojotrees-versus-LightGBM differential has ever been RECORDED on this scenario's synthetic variant; both stored runs carry the real variant only. 0.025 is therefore derived from the real variant's measured differential and from the size of the regression it must catch, not from the synthetic variant's own noise. If the synthetic variant turns out to disagree with LightGBM by more than this for a reason that is not a regression, the number needs revisiting in a commit that says so. It does not need revisiting by being quietly raised on the morning it first goes red.

baseline.rationale: The constant baseline scores 0.5 by construction. A model below 0.65 has found almost nothing and its agreement with another such model says nothing.

differential.rationale: Multiclass compounds: one tree per class per round, and a divergence in round one is carried by every later round through the softmax. Five percent allows for that accumulation where three would fail on drift alone.

baseline.rationale: The baseline is the class prior, which is a strong opponent on a skewed problem. Ten percent is enough to show the trees are contributing.

differential.rationale: The loosest threshold in the file, and the caveats on the scenario say why: LightGBM reads its pairwise sigmoid from a lookup table where mojotrees evaluates it, so the two models diverge from the first pair rather than from the first tie. Comparable NDCG is the claim being tested, not identical models.

baseline.rationale: The baseline leaves every query in stored order, which on a real ranking file is not random and can score surprisingly well. Five points above it is the floor for having learned anything.

differential.rationale: Category-set splits are chosen by sorting categories on a smoothed gradient statistic and taking a prefix, and two implementations of that sort break ties differently on a high-cardinality column. Missing direction is decided per node and can flip on a near-tie. Both are genuine divergence sources, so this is looser than the dense case.

baseline.rationale: The categorical signal in the generator is most of the variance, so a model that handled categories as ordinal numbers would still beat the mean. Fifteen percent, not twenty, so this checks for a fit rather than for a good one.

adult.rationale: The real variant of this scenario is a classification problem. 0.85 AUC on adult is well inside what a gradient-boosted model reaches, so a run below it has a data or encoding fault rather than a modelling one.

differential.rationale: Both engines see the same CSC matrix with the same zero semantics, and neither is doing feature bundling. The remaining difference is which of many near-identical sparse columns wins a split, which moves AUC in the third decimal place.

baseline.rationale: Signal is concentrated in a few hundred of tens of thousands of columns. A model that missed them lands near 0.5, and 0.70 separates that clearly from a model that found them.

differential.rationale: The widest gate in this file and the most asymmetric, and both properties are deliberate. mojotrees keeps at most max_bin - 1 = 254 categories per column and lumps every other code into a bin that can never join a split set (src/mojotrees/categorical.mojo, 'Capacity'); LightGBM's max_bin is a FLOOR on a categorical column's bin count and it keeps admitting categories until it has both covered 99 percent of the rows and spent max_bin bins. On this scenario's standard tier that is 254 bins against roughly 100,000 on one column and 254 against 20,000 on another. That is a known structural deficit on our side, sized before any run, and a gate tight enough to fail on it would fail on the first run for a reason nobody needed a benchmark to learn. 0.05 absolute AUC bounds it loosely enough to still catch a broken model.
differential.why_asymmetric: implausible_better is 0.02 against a max_worse of 0.05, which is the only inverted pair in this file. mojotrees is structurally handicapped on this scenario by the capacity ceiling above, so a LARGE win is stronger evidence that the two engines were not given the same problem than it is anywhere else. Small wins remain plausible and are not caught: mojotrees uses exact row counts where LightGBM estimates a bin's count from its Hessian sum, and mojotrees drops no rare category where LightGBM drops everything under min_data_in_bin.
differential.exit_condition: this number comes down to the dense case's band the day a mojotrees categorical column stops being capped at 254 levels. An ordered target statistic does that by turning the column into one numeric feature of 255 bins, which is the whole reason that mechanism is being built, so a tightening here is the measurable form of that lane landing. Loosening it further needs a commit that says why.
differential.known_risk: no mojotrees-versus-LightGBM differential has ever been recorded on this scenario, at any tier, because it did not exist before 2026-08-16. 0.05 is derived from the capacity gap above and from nothing measured. If the first run comes in wildly outside it, the number to question is this one and the place to question it is a commit, not the morning it goes red.

baseline.rationale: The generator puts most of the signal in five categorical columns and a double-centered two-column interaction, at a 10 percent positive rate. A constant model scores 0.5. 0.70 separates a model that found the categorical structure from one that treated the codes as ordinal numbers, which is the failure this scenario is built to expose, and it does not assert that either engine fitted it well.
baseline.why_this_number: measured rather than guessed, and measured without training anything. On 2026-08-16 a cat_smooth-smoothed per-level target mean, fitted on the training split and scored on the held-out split at 200,000 rows with the cardinality ladder divided by five, reaches 0.8165 AUC from the five categorical columns alone, against 0.6338 from the numeric terms alone. A boosted model with both should sit above that, so 0.70 is a floor with real margin under it rather than a floor sitting on top of the achievable value. See scenarios.HIGH_CARDINALITY_LEVELS for the per-column readings.

differential.rationale: The same data recipe as dense_regression at the same objective and the same bin count, so the same reasoning and the same numbers apply: what is left between mojotrees and LightGBM is split-search tie breaking and floating-point summation order. This gate is against the COMPARATOR and is unaffected by anything CatBoost resolves; the ordered-boosting question this scenario exists for lives in a peer column, and nothing in this file is measured against a peer column.

baseline.rationale: dense_regression's floor, for dense_regression's reason: a model that cannot beat the training mean did not fit, and two engines agreeing on a non-model would otherwise pass the differential check. This scenario runs the generator at a higher noise level (0.60 against 0.30) so that a 100-tree model at 50,000 rows genuinely overfits, which lowers the achievable improvement; 0.15 was already loosened once against measured data and is not lowered again here on an argument. If the noise level turns out to put it out of reach, the fix is a commit that says so.

rationale: No timing in this harness fails a run, on purpose.
The machine this is most likely to run on is a laptop that throttles,
shares its memory bandwidth with a browser, and is sometimes on
battery. A ratio measured there is a fact about that afternoon.
